- Asset-light wholesale trading model requiring comparatively lower capital expenditure than pharmaceutical manufacturing; the Company states it does not own any significant fixed assets
- Debt-free capital structure - the Company states it continues to maintain a debt-free capital structure, and the debt-equity and debt service coverage ratios are disclosed as not applicable as no debt has been raised

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Unproven business transformation - the pharmaceutical trading business is still at inception with essentially no revenue behind it — The Company changed its principal business from Information Technology and software services to the trading of pharmaceutical, hygiene and cleanroom products during FY2025-26 and states it 'is presently in the initial stage of business transformation' and 'in the initial phase of developing its pharmaceutical trading business'. Its FY2025-26 revenue from operations still came from the legacy technology business (Projects & Services and Software Sales), so sourcing arrangements, the distribution network and the customer base all remain to be built. Management's outlook rests on industry fundamentals rather than an established book of business.
- Regulatory compliance risk in one of India's most regulated sectors — Management states that wholesale distributors must comply with regulations on drug licensing, storage conditions, product traceability, GST compliance and quality standards under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and related regulations, and that any change in regulatory requirements may increase compliance costs and impact operations. Changes in healthcare regulations and product quality risk are also listed among the business risks.
- Pricing pressure and thin trading margins — The MD&A flags increasing pressure on product pricing from government regulation under the Drug Price Control Order (DPCO), competition among distributors and procurement by institutional buyers, and states that 'sustaining profitability while maintaining competitive pricing remains a key challenge'. For a pure trading model with no manufacturing value-add, margin is the whole economics.
- Supply chain and sourcing dependency on third-party manufacturers — The distribution business depends on timely procurement and uninterrupted supply from manufacturers; the Company flags that disruption from raw material shortages, transportation bottlenecks, geopolitical developments or manufacturing delays may impact product availability and customer service. The Company has no manufacturing of its own and is still establishing supplier relationships.
- Working capital intensity and customer credit / liquidity risk against a very small equity base — Management states the wholesale pharmaceutical business generally requires adequate working capital to hold inventory and extend credit to customers, and separately recognises risks relating to customer credit, liquidity management and operational continuity. Shareholders' funds fell to Rs.17.88 Lakhs as on 31st March 2026 from Rs.63.95 Lakhs a year earlier because of the year's loss, and the Company reports no debt raised, so the balance sheet supporting any inventory-and-receivables build is thin.
- Intense competition from organised and unorganised distributors — The Indian pharmaceutical distribution market is described as comprising several organised and unorganised players competing on pricing, product availability and customer service; the Company is a new entrant with no established distribution footprint, and management says continuous improvement in operational efficiency, customer relationships and product portfolio will be essential to remain competitive.
- Listing-compliance lapse - a penalty charged by BSE Limited materially affected the year's result — The MD&A attributes the FY2025-26 loss to higher employee benefit expenses, administrative costs and 'penalties incurred during the year', and the note to the key-ratio table states explicitly that the change in profitability and margin ratios is 'mainly due to the reason that the profit / (loss) for the current year is impacted due to penalty charged by BSE Limited and increased employee benefit expenses'. This is a disclosed compliance failure with a real earnings consequence, not process boilerplate.
- Change of control and near-complete turnover of the board and key managerial personnel — June Enterprises Private Limited acquired 60.88% of the share capital under the promoter category via a Share Purchase Agreement dated 05 March 2025 and a SEBI (SAST) open offer, making the Company its subsidiary. Across FY2025-26 the entire executive and much of the non-executive bench changed: the Managing Director, a Director who was also Chief Financial Officer, and another Director resigned effective 24th May 2025, two more directors resigned w.e.f. 14th August 2025, a new MD and Whole-Time Director were appointed w.e.f. 23rd May 2025, three Independent Directors w.e.f. 21st July 2025, and both the CFO and the Company Secretary & Compliance Officer positions changed hands during the year. Sixteen board meetings were required. Execution of the new strategy depends entirely on an untested management team.
- Single-segment, single-activity concentration — The Company states it presently operates in a single business segment so segment-wise reporting is not applicable, and it is simultaneously exiting its legacy activity. There is no second line of business to absorb a setback in the pharmaceutical trading build-out.

business.body: The Company is a public limited company incorporated in India and listed on BSE Limited, with its registered office in Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra and its corporate office in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. During the year under review it changed its principal business activity to the trading of pharmaceutical, hygiene and cleanroom products, and is presently in the initial phase of establishing sourcing arrangements, a distribution network and relationships with manufacturers, healthcare institutions and retail customers. Its residual operating revenue in FY2025-26 still came from the legacy technology business, comprising income from Projects & Services and Software Sales; the Company operates in a single business segment, so segment-wise reporting is stated to be not applicable.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The annual report describes no plant, capacity or capital-expenditure project. June Industries is explicitly an asset-light wholesale trading business: management states that the Company's wholesale trading model 'enables it to operate with comparatively lower capital expenditure requirements than pharmaceutical manufacturing businesses', and that as per the audited financial statements for the year ended 31st March 2026 the Company 'does not own any significant fixed assets'. Expansion is framed entirely as commercial build-out rather than physical capacity: following the shareholder-approved change of main object (postal ballot notice dated 14th August 2025) from Information Technology and software services to the trading of pharmaceutical, hygiene and cleanroom products, the Company says it is in the initial phase of establishing reliable sourcing arrangements, strengthening its distribution network and building long-term relationships with manufacturers, healthcare institutions and retail customers. It intends to gradually widen the portfolio to pharmaceutical formulations, hygiene products, cleanroom consumables and other healthcare-related products, to explore specialised healthcare products and hygiene solutions to diversify revenue streams, and to enhance operational efficiency through technology-driven processes (ERP, digital inventory management, online procurement platforms). The only stated physical footprint is the registered office in Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra and the corporate office in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. No commissioning dates, no capacity additions, no project names and no rupee capex quantum are disclosed.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Management states India continues to be one of the fastest-growing pharmaceutical markets globally, recognised as the 'Pharmacy of the World', supplying medicines to more than 200 countries
- The Indian pharmaceutical market is estimated to have crossed USD 65 billion during FY 2025-26 and is expected to reach nearly USD 130 billion by 2030, driven by increasing healthcare expenditure, rising life expectancy, expansion of health insurance coverage and increasing prevalence of chronic diseases
- Government initiatives cited as demand drivers: Ayushman Bharat, the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Pharmaceuticals, Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana and continued investment in healthcare infrastructure
- Shift of pharmaceutical distribution from fragmented unorganised players to organised wholesale distributors that comply with regulatory standards, maintain traceability and ensure timely delivery - management sees this as the opening for professionally managed companies
- Increasing demand from expansion of organised retail pharmacies, growth of e-pharmacies, improved logistics infrastructure and digital supply chain management systems
- Growing awareness of infection prevention, workplace hygiene, pharmaceutical manufacturing standards and healthcare safety is raising demand for hygiene products and cleanroom consumables
- Growing institutional demand from hospitals, clinics and healthcare providers expected to support long-term business growth
- Headwinds management flags against these drivers: pricing pressure under the Drug Price Control Order (DPCO) and institutional procurement, regulatory compliance cost, supply chain disruption, working capital intensity of wholesale distribution, and intense competition from organised and unorganised players
- Management notes the Company is presently in the initial stage of business transformation, so the outlook rests on industry fundamentals rather than on an established book of business
